summary: This standards-track document extends IMAP so a server can search mail with inexact matching. The server also gives each matching message a relevancy score, so the best matches can be shown first. It is meant for typical search where spelling and word forms vary.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of finding only exact words, your mail program can ask for messages that roughly match and sort them from best to worst, like a search engine does.

questions: how to rank imap search results
how does imap relevancy score work
subtitle: An IMAP extension that lets servers match mail loosely and score each hit by relevancy.

tldr.problem: People searching their mail want the most relevant results first, but plain IMAP SEARCH only matches exactly and gives no ranking.
tldr.mechanism: A new FUZZY search key lets the server match however it sees fit, and a RELEVANCY score from 1 to 100 can be returned or used for sorting.
tldr.outcome: Servers that advertise SEARCH=FUZZY can return ranked, inexact matches, but results are deliberately not guaranteed to be repeatable.

facts.label: New sort key and return option

today: RFC 6203 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Fuzzy Search
sections.content:
When people search mail in an IMAP client, they usually want the most relevant results first. RFC 6203 says a server can do this most efficiently when it is free to decide internally how a search matches messages.

The document defines a new IMAP capability, SEARCH=FUZZY, that provides this. It is a Standards Track extension to the IMAP SEARCH command.
sections.plainLanguage: When you look for a toy in a messy room, you want the likely ones first, not only the one with the exact label.

sections.title: The FUZZY Search Key
sections.content:
The FUZZY search key takes another search key as its argument. For that key the server may match in any implementation-defined way, including ignoring the active comparator from RFC 5255. It is typically used on strings. In the RFC's example, SEARCH FUZZY (SUBJECT "IMAP break") may also match subjects such as "broken IMAP" or "IMAP is broken".

Only the key wrapped by FUZZY is fuzzy. In SEARCH FUZZY SUBJECT work FROM user@example.com, the subject search is fuzzy and the FROM search is exact. How a server treats several separate FUZZY keys is implementation-defined.

Fuzzy results can differ for the same user at different times, or between users. The RFC gives examples such as a search that adapts to a user's habits, or load balancing. Clients need to warn users that fuzzy results are not necessarily deterministic.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the server which clue can be a bit loose. The server may bring back things that nearly match, and it might not give the same answer every time.

sections.title: Relevancy Scores
sections.content:
Servers SHOULD give each matched message a relevancy score from 1 to 100 when FUZZY is used, where 100 is the most relevant. They SHOULD use the whole range so clients can show it meaningfully, for example as a percentage.

Relevancy is not the same as how precisely a message matched. A message whose subject fuzzily matches may score higher than one with the exact string in the middle of a sentence in its body. How a score is calculated across several fuzzy keys depends on the server.

If the server also advertises ESEARCH (RFC 4731), a client can ask for scores with the RELEVANCY return option, as in SEARCH RETURN (RELEVANCY ALL) FUZZY TEXT "Helo". The option MUST NOT be used without a FUZZY key. Plain SEARCH results are not sorted by relevancy; SORT is needed for that.
sections.plainLanguage: Each result gets a grade from 1 to 100, like a score on a quiz. A higher grade means a better match.

sections.title: Fuzzy Matching Beyond Strings
sections.content:
Fuzzy matching is not limited to text. All search keys SHOULD be matched fuzzily, but what that means is left to the server, which may decide it is meaningless for a key and fall back to exact matching. The RFC offers suggestions:

  • Dates: a search for a message "from Dave about a week ago" could return messages outside the date range, with lower scores the further away they are.
  • Sizes: handled like dates, for example "about 1 MB attachments" using LARGER 900000 SMALLER 1100000.
  • Flags: messages without the flag, such as ANSWERED, could be returned with lower scores.
  • UIDs, sequences and modification sequences: exact matching probably makes sense, though a server might widen a UID range by 5% on each side.
sections.plainLanguage: Fuzzy can work on dates and sizes too. If you say about a week ago, a message from eight days ago still counts, just with a lower grade.

sections.title: Extensions to SORT and SEARCH
sections.content:
If the server advertises SORT (RFC 5256), the new RELEVANCY sort criterion orders results with the highest score first. As with the return option, it MUST NOT be used without a FUZZY key.

With ESORT from RFC 5267, scores can be returned with SORT RETURN (RELEVANCY ALL). If the server advertises CONTEXT=SORT or CONTEXT=SEARCH, the PARTIAL return option can limit the result, for example to the 10 most relevant messages.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask the server to line up the results with the best grade first, and even to give you only the top ten.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The syntax extends the IMAP grammar in ABNF. It adds the capability name SEARCH=FUZZY, the search key FUZZY SP search-key, the return option and sort key RELEVANCY, and the returned data RELEVANCY SP score-list. A score is one to three digits with a value from 1 to 100, and a score-list is a parenthesized, space-separated list of them.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is the exact spelling of the new words, so every server and mail program writes them the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Fuzzy search engines are often complex, with non-obvious disk, memory and CPU usage, so the extension might enable denial-of-service attacks. Servers MAY limit the resources a single search or user can use. Implementors should test with large messages containing very long words or unique random strings, since very long search keys might also use excessive memory or CPU.

Invalid input can be a problem too. For example, illegal UTF-8 in a message claiming to be UTF-8 could be replaced with the Unicode replacement character (U+FFFD).

Relevancy rankings might be "poisoned" by attackers using certain keywords or hidden markup such as HTML to boost rankings. Servers cannot fully prevent this, so clients should let users see all results rather than hiding those below a certain score.
sections.plainLanguage: A very clever search can use up the server's strength, and sneaky senders can try to make their mail look extra important. So servers set limits and mail programs should still show everything.

data.title: Sorting fuzzy results
data.code:
C: C1 SORT (RELEVANCY) UTF-8 FUZZY SUBJECT "Helo"
S: * SORT 5 10 1
S: C1 OK Sort completed.
